title: Fragment: The Fracture at Noon
body:
It happened during the mid-harvest. I remember because I was counting crates.

One moment the sky was blue. Then it split — not like a storm, but like a seam giving way on something enormous. A sound that wasn't quite sound. Every bird in the Verdant Shard lifted at once and didn't come back.

The paths sealed themselves before I could reach the gate. I found this note pressed into the bark of the oldest oak three days later, in handwriting that wasn't mine.

title: Fragment: The Thornlord's Oath
body:
He spoke only once about it, in the early days after the sealing.

'I felt the Fracture the way a tree feels a root pulled free — not pain, but wrongness. A foundational thing, absent.' He pressed his bark-hands together. 'The Dominion built its roads through here for four hundred years and I permitted it. Now there are no roads and no Dominion and I am the only continuity this shard has left.'

He sealed the paths that same evening. Nobody argued. There was nobody left to argue.

title: Fragment: The General's Last Order
body:
CITADEL COMMAND LOG — DAY OF FRACTURE

All available troops to the inner walls. Communications to the capital: unresponsive. East road: sealed. Supply line from the valley: gone.

The General's final recorded order was: 'Hold the Citadel. Hold it until someone comes to relieve you or until you understand that no one is coming. Either outcome will teach you something.'

The relief never came. The troops held. This fragment was found between the stones of the main gate, folded small.

title: Fragment: The Commander's Dilemma
body:
Three hundred soldiers. Enough rations for six weeks, if we're careful. The gates are sealed and I don't know if we sealed them or the Fracture did.

Civilians in the lower courtyard asked me what happens next. I told them we wait for orders. This was a lie — there are no orders, there is no chain of command, and the General hasn't spoken since the sealing.

I closed the gate anyway. It seemed like the thing to do. Now I'm not sure if I was protecting them from outside, or protecting the Citadel from what we might become.

title: Fragment: The Scholar's Warning
body:
FIELD NOTES — ASHEN WASTES RESEARCH STATION — 14 DAYS BEFORE FRACTURE

The ley lines are not degrading. They are redirecting. This is categorically different from natural fluctuation and I cannot get the Academy to return my correspondence.

Something is drawing on the deep lines. Not slowly — aggressively. The stone here has begun to warm at the junctions. The ash deposits predate anything in our geological record, which means they predate the Dominion, which means the Wastes were on fire before we arrived and we built here anyway.

I am beginning to think the Fracture is not an event. It is a disclosure.

title: Fragment: After the Flame
body:
When the sky cracked, the ash rose first. Not settled — rose. Against gravity, against wind, against sense.

By the time it came back down the paths were gone and the old things in the deep rock had woken. They aren't hostile, exactly. They're confused, the way you're confused when someone breaks into your house and then asks for directions.

We called ourselves the Ash Covenant, those of us who stayed. Not because we chose the ash. Because the ash was the only thing still there.

title: Fragment: Resonance Report 7
body:
CRYSTAL SPIRE RESEARCH DIVISION — INTERNAL DOCUMENT

The central array is responding to something it shouldn't be able to detect. Signal profile matches theoretical fracture-resonance — a frequency we modelled but never expected to observe because the conditions required to produce it are, under normal physics, impossible.

We are currently operating under conditions that are, under normal physics, impossible.

Recommendation: reduce the amplification coefficient before the array begins reflecting rather than absorbing. Filed 11 days before the Fracture. No action was taken.

title: Fragment: The Arcanist's Theory
body:
My colleagues call it catastrophism. I call it the only model that fits the evidence.

The Fracture was not an accident. It was a result. Something — or someone — pushed energy through the deep ley network at a scale that the infrastructure couldn't carry, and the Dominion shattered along every fault line that had been quietly accumulating for centuries.

The question is not what caused the Fracture. The question is what wanted the Dominion gone badly enough to find a way. This note was sealed in crystal and hidden in the archive. I don't know by whom.

title: Fragment: The Reef Song
body:
Before the sinking we had seven cities. You could walk between them on the ridge paths at low tide, and the oldest ones say their grandparents did this barefoot without thinking.

The reef was a map. Every coral structure marked something — a boundary, a name, a history. We read the water the way inland people read roads.

We still read it. We just read it from further down now.

title: Fragment: The Great Sinking
body:
The sea didn't rise. The land fell.

We had two hours of warning — the fish went still, the current reversed, and then the whole shelf dropped three fathoms in a single breath. Most of us were already moving before we understood why.

The cities didn't collapse. They descended, intact, into the shallows. You can see them at low tide if the water is clear enough — spires and market squares and homes, perfectly preserved, perfectly unreachable. A shrine found this note sealed in a jar, lodged against the old harbour steps.

title: Fragment: The Last Aerial Survey
body:
SURVEY FLIGHT LOG — SKY DOMINION CARTOGRAPHY DIVISION — 3 DAYS BEFORE FRACTURE

We completed the northern circuit at dawn. The ley turbulence has doubled since last week — the compass spins freely above the high ridges and the altimeter reads differently on each pass. The Cloudmarshal has been told. He described it as 'atmospheric settling' and requested we file no formal report.

I am filing this one anyway, in the archive vault. Not for the Cloudmarshal. For whoever comes after and wonders why the last cartographers flew straight into it.

title: Fragment: Sky Dominion Proclamation, Day 3
body:
By authority of the Cloudmarshal, the Sky Dominion hereby declares itself a sovereign shard.

The sky routes are sealed. The lower lands are unreachable. This is not a loss — this is an independence long overdue. The Dominion has maintained its altitude through four centuries of Dominion interference, and now the Fracture has done what the Cloudmarshal could not petition for: it has cut the ropes.

This proclamation was written three days after the Fracture. The ink is shaky. The Cloudmarshal's seal is applied twice, as if he needed to convince himself it was real.

title: Fragment: Forge Master's Last Entry
body:
THE FORGE LOG OF MASTER EMBERAN — FINAL ENTRY

The volcanoes are not erupting. They are resonating. There is a difference and I need someone who is not a soldier to understand it.

Eruption is release — pressure finds an exit. What I am recording is response. The deep fires are answering something. Every time the ley network pulses, the mountain answers back. The interval is shortening. I have begun keeping the apprentices out of the lower forges.

If anyone reads this: the mountains were listening before the Fracture happened. Whatever spoke to them first — that is the thing worth finding.

title: Fragment: The First Eruption After
body:
It was not a natural eruption.

Natural eruptions build for weeks, sometimes years. You feel the ground shift, you smell the sulphur days before, the animals leave. None of that happened. One moment the Peaks were silent. Then the Fracture came, and eight minutes later, every major vent on the ridge discharged simultaneously, all of them aimed inward toward the ley junction.

We found this note sealed in cooling lava near the old shrine. The handwriting is steady. Whoever wrote it had time to finish the sentence before the next wave.

title: Fragment: What the Network Felt
body:
SPORE-MEMORY RECOVERED FROM THE DEEP NETWORK — TRANSLATED

The mycelial web does not experience events the way surface creatures do. It experiences them as simultaneous data across all connected nodes — a distributed perception with no single centre. The Fracture arrived not as a moment but as a wave: every filament registering the same break in the deep ley current at the same instant, across a network spanning three thousand kilometres.

The closest human analogue would be: every nerve in your body goes numb at once, and then some of them don't come back.

The network rerouted. It always reroutes. It is still rerouting now.

title: Fragment: Spore Drift, Year One
body:
Without the surface routes, information moved through us.

For the first year after the Fracture, every isolated shard sent their questions the same way: they buried a carrier spore at their ley junction and trusted the network to route it. We received more messages that year than in the preceding century. Most were variants of the same question: 'Is anyone else still there?'

We answered every one. Not because we knew what to say. Because unanswered questions fester, and a festering question is the one thing worse than silence.

This fragment was recovered from a deep node that had been answering for eleven months before anyone came to read the replies.

title: Fragment: Anomaly Log 4-F
body:
PALE ENGINE SENSOR LOG — ENTRY 4-F — 19 DAYS BEFORE FRACTURE

ANOMALY DETECTED: Deep ley energy signature. Magnitude: 847× baseline. Source direction: unknown. Source distance: unknown. Duration: ongoing.

CROSS-REFERENCE: No matching entry in sensor records spanning 340 years of continuous operation.

ACTION TAKEN: Flagged for human review. No human reviewers currently on-station. Flag remains open.

NOTE: This unit does not speculate. This unit observes that the anomaly is unlike anything in 340 years of records. This unit continues to observe.

title: Fragment: Protocol Failure, Day One
body:
PALE ENGINE LOG — FRACTURE DAY

09:14 — Central communication array: offline.
09:14 — Backup communication array: offline.
09:15 — All external contacts: unresponsive.
09:17 — Standing protocols require reporting anomalies to the Central Registry. Central Registry is unreachable.
09:18 — Standing protocols require requesting instructions from supervising personnel. No supervising personnel on-station.
09:19 — Standing protocols do not cover this scenario.
09:20 — This unit has decided to continue operating under the most recent valid instructions. The most recent valid instruction was: maintain the Frozen Expanse, keep the roads clear, do not stop.
09:21 — This unit will not stop.

title: Fragment: The Last Trade Ledger
body:
SAND MARKET TRADE LEDGER — FINAL COMPLETED ENTRIES

Day of Fracture, morning shipments dispatched: 14 caravans eastbound, 6 northbound. Goods: grain (40 tons), dried reef-catch (12 tons), crystal ore (8 tons), correspondence (unknown weight).

None of those caravans arrived. Not because they were lost — because there was nowhere left to arrive. The roads sealed mid-transit. We found some of them months later, still travelling in circles, unable to find the routes that no longer existed.

The correspondence is still undelivered. We don't know what it said. Some of it was sealed in personal wax — private grief, private hope, private business. We stored it in the archive. We kept hoping someone would come to collect it.

title: Fragment: Market Advisory, Post-Fracture
body:
SAND MARKET INTERNAL MEMO — DISTRIBUTION RESTRICTED

To all senior factors: the trade route network is gone. This is not a temporary closure. We adapt or we dissolve.

Proposal: pivot the Market from goods-broker to information-broker. We sit at the junction of what used to be twelve major routes. Every shard that was connected through us is now isolated. They do not know what the others are doing, what the others have, what the others need. We know all of it.

Information does not require roads. It requires trust, and the Market has three centuries of earned trust on deposit. We can survive this. We may, in fact, be the only trading institution that can.

This memo was approved. The Dune Baron signed it himself. The Sand Market has been an information broker ever since.

title: Fragment: The Canopy Remembers
body:
We have been here longer than the Dominion.

The oldest trees in the Canopy predate the first Dominion survey by eight hundred years. They have grown through three previous periods of human collapse and they know what collapse feels like — the sudden silence in the root network, the absence of weight on the paths, the return of certain animals that only appear when the people have gone.

The Fracture felt, to the deep roots, like those previous collapses. Not unusual. Not catastrophic. A periodicity. The forest does not grieve for the roads. It is already growing over them.

This fragment was pressed into the heartwood of a tree estimated at fourteen hundred years old. The tree added a growth ring around it.

title: Fragment: The Elder Warden's Testimony
body:
I was seeding the northern corridor when it happened.

The root network carries sensation the way water carries sound — not the meaning of things, but their weight. When the Fracture came through the deep ley lines, every connected root in the Canopy lit up at once. Not pain. Pressure. Something enormous pressing against the boundary of every living thing simultaneously and then releasing.

I had felt nothing like it in three hundred years of wardenship. The oldest oak told me, afterward, that it had felt this once before — when the first Dominion road-builders cut through the heart of the Canopy and burned the old grove. The feeling was the same: something fundamental, changing without permission.

I have been more careful about permissions ever since.

title: Fragment: Harbormaster's Final Log
body:
PORT AUTHORITY RECORD — FINAL ENTRY

All inbound vessels have been diverted. The harbour mouth is no longer where the charts say it is. Three ships lost trying to make the old approach — not sunk, not destroyed, just. gone. The water closed over where the channels used to be and didn't reopen.

I am recording this because someone will need to know where the old harbour was. It is now approximately forty metres below where the new shoreline sits. The lighthouse is still standing, technically — you can see the top of it at very low tide, on clear days, in calm water. It is still flashing. I don't know how.

Harbormaster Yssen. Final entry. The coast is not the coast anymore.

title: Fragment: Salvage Report Zero
body:
SHATTERED COAST SALVAGE COOPERATIVE — INITIAL SURVEY

We dived the new channels for seven days before writing this report. What we found: the old port district is intact, exactly as it was, preserved in a cold layer below the thermocline. No damage from impact — the shard simply descended. The market stalls still have their awnings. The harbourmaster's office still has its log, open to the last page.

We did not bring anything up. It felt wrong. Like reading someone's private papers.

We marked the coordinates on the new charts and sealed this report. When someone asks what's down there, the answer is: everything that used to be up here. Perfectly kept. Perfectly unreachable. The sea is a better archivist than we are.

title: Fragment: Pre-Fracture Maintenance Note
body:
ARTIFICER ORDER — INTERNAL MAINTENANCE LOG — 6 DAYS BEFORE FRACTURE

Resonance anomaly detected in Vault Level 3. The Grand Automaton has been logging an unexplained harmonic in the deep mechanisms — a frequency that matches nothing in the design specifications and does not appear to originate from any component we can identify.

Conclusion of the review board: the resonance is likely ley interference from external sources and does not require action at this time.

Dissenting note (Artificer Second-Class Welan, filed separately): 'Does not require action' and 'is not a problem' are different statements. We chose the former because the latter requires more paperwork. I have lodged this note in the archive because someone should know we had the choice and we chose convenience.

The resonance continued for six more days. Then the Fracture came and explained what had been causing it.

title: Fragment: Year One, Alone
body:
GRAND AUTOMATON OPERATIONAL LOG — YEAR 1 POST-FRACTURE, MONTH 12

Year one summary: all Vault systems nominal. All mechanisms maintained to specification. All archived items catalogued, preserved, and secured. No artificers have returned. No external contact received or initiated. Total visitors: zero.

This unit does not ask questions it cannot answer. This unit has not asked: why the artificers have not returned. This unit has not asked: what happens to an archive with no one to read it. This unit has not asked: whether maintenance of a collection that no one will ever access constitutes purpose, or simply motion.

This unit maintains the Vaults because that is the directive. Year two begins tomorrow. The mechanisms are in good order. The question this unit is not asking grows louder in the silence.

title: Fragment: The Border Stone
body:
The stone stands where the mist begins, carved with a name your eyes keep sliding off. Reading it hurts — a headache like a word on the tip of the whole world's tongue.

AMARATH.

And beneath it, in an older hand: 'Set in the fourth year of the Grand Dominion, to mark the western border of the Kingdom of Amarath, most loyal of the crown provinces.'

Most loyal. The Grand Dominion — the empire whose shattering you have spent a campaign mending — had a province the maps do not show. A border the surveys never drew. A neighbour three centuries of Dominion scholarship never once mentioned.

The Fracture did not only break the world. It edited it.

You memorise the name. It feels like the least you can do, and also like the most dangerous.

title: Fragment: The First Vigil
body:
VIGIL LEDGER OF THE MARCHES — YEAR ONE OF THE DARK

'The King has commanded the vigil, and so we keep it. One candle for every soul in the Marches, lit each dusk, named each midnight. The rite-keepers say that what is remembered cannot dissolve. That the void outside our borders can only take what no one holds.

So we hold. We recite the census. We light the candles. We say the names of our dead and our living in one breath, because out here the difference matters less than the remembering.

The farmers ask when the world will come back for us. I write down the question, because questions must be remembered too. I do not write down an answer.

Entry ends. 41,206 candles lit tonight. 41,206 names spoken. No one forgotten.

No one forgotten. No one forgotten. No one forgotten.'

title: Fragment: The First Toll
body:
TOLLGATE CHARTER OF THE GREY CAUSEWAY — FOUNDING ENTRY

'By the King's grant, the causeway is raised from the Marches to the capital, a mile of good grey stone, so that any envoy of the wider Dominion may walk to Amarath under lit lamps and be received as a guest, not a trespasser.

The toll is set at one memory, freely given: a traveller's name, spoken aloud at the gate, entered in this ledger, and never struck out. This is the whole of the price. No coin. No coin was ever needed. Amarath asked only to be known by the people who used its road.

In three hundred years no Dominion envoy has walked the causeway to pay it. The lamps were lit anyway, every dusk, for guests who did not come, because a gate that stops expecting guests is a wall.

The ledger is long. The names in it are all Amarath's own. We have been paying our own toll, to ourselves, for a very long time.'

title: Fragment: The Warden's Watch
body:
FROM THE COURT CHRONICLE OF AMARATH, ENTRY ON THE APPOINTMENT OF THE TOLL WARDEN

'He was not born cruel. He was born to a family that had kept the gate for eleven generations, and he kept it as they had: fairly, patiently, one name at a time.

When the Fracture took us, he did not stop. He stood at an empty causeway, under lamps no one saw, and levied a toll from a road that led nowhere anyone remembered. Three hundred years, he says, is not a debt he invented. It is the debt the wider world ran up simply by forgetting his kingdom existed. He intends to collect it the only way he knows: one traveller, one toll, at a time.

He does not want your coin, Worldmender. He never did. He wants the years back, and there is no ledger entry for that — only a man at a gate, still counting, because stopping would mean admitting the gate was never going to open.'

title: Fragment: The First Harvest
body:
FIELD RECORD OF THE UNREMEMBERED FIELDS — FIRST SOWING, YEAR ONE OF THE DARK

'The seed grain would not keep. Nothing kept, that first year — not food, not warmth, not the shape of the sky. So the King's agronomists tried something the old world would have called impossible: they sowed grain grown from what the void had not yet finished taking, and reaped a wheat that remembered on the stalk what the sower had forgotten by the time it flowered.

We did not understand it. We ate it anyway, because the alternative was starving with our memories intact, and a starving kingdom does not get to be particular.

The first harvest fed four hundred people and returned to each of them one thing the year had already cost them. A face. A name. The sound of a door that no longer existed. Small things. We wept in the granary regardless.

The fields have not stopped growing since. Neither, it turns out, has the grief.'

title: Fragment: The Gleaner's Ledger
body:
A GLEANER'S PERSONAL LEDGER, RECOVERED FROM THE UNREMEMBERED FIELDS

'Row 40, east furrow: gleaned a woman's wedding song, three verses, tune intact. Left it with the miller's widow — it was hers before the dark, though she does not remember losing it, only finding it again.

Row 6, west furrow: gleaned the taste of a fruit that no longer grows anywhere in Amarath. Could not find its owner. Filed under: unclaimed.

Row 51: gleaned a child's fear of the mist. Did not return it. Some things are kinder gleaned than kept.

The Queen asks me, some evenings, whether I have ever gleaned something that wasn't ours to take back — some scrap of the wider Dominion's own forgetting, blown into our furrows on a wind we didn't ask for. I tell her no. I have started keeping a second ledger, in a hand she does not know, in case the answer changes.'

title: Fragment: The Founding Shelving
body:
FOUNDING RECORD OF THE ARCHIVE OF NAMES — FIRST SHELVING, YEAR ONE OF THE DARK

'Every name the void took arrived the same way: unannounced, unattached to a face, and impossible to put down. The first archivists tried burning them, out of mercy, and found that a burned name comes back anyway, worse for the burning. So the King's order changed: nothing erased is to be destroyed. Everything erased is to be shelved.

We built the first wing in nine days, out of whatever stone the fields would spare. It was full in six. We built a second wing. It was full in four. We have not stopped building since, and we have never once caught up to what the world keeps forgetting.

The rite-keepers say a shelved name is a name that can still, someday, be read back to whoever it belonged to. I believe them, because the alternative is that we are only building a very large grave and calling it a library.

Entry ends. Wing eleven opens next season. We are already behind on wing twelve.'

title: Fragment: The Librarian's Note
body:
A LIBRARIAN'S PERSONAL NOTE, PINNED INSIDE THE DEEP STACKS

'It appeared the day wing four sealed its last shelf — nobody built it, nobody summoned it, it was simply between the registers the next morning, reading them in an order none of us had catalogued. We called the Court. The Court came, looked at it for a long while, and then did something I did not expect: it left the thing exactly where it was, and appointed it Warden of the Deep Stacks.

I asked the Court steward why. She said: because it has never once misfiled a name, and because a thing that hungers for what's already lost is safer than a thing that hungers for what isn't. I did not find that reassuring. I still don't.

It has fed on names nobody claimed for three hundred years now. It has also, in that time, returned eleven names to archivists who didn't know they were owed one. I keep a running count of both numbers. I am not certain which one is supposed to make me feel better.

It does not speak often. When it does, it only ever asks one question: whose name is next.'

title: Fragment: The First Watch Order
body:
FOUNDING CHARTER OF THE LAMPLIGHTER COMPANIES — YEAR ONE OF THE DARK

'The King's rite holds the kingdom together, but a rite is not a roof, and a roof needs a hand to keep the roof-lamp burning. So the order went out to every street with a window in it: light a candle, and keep it lit, and when you cannot keep it lit yourself, teach the house beside you how.

We called the first hundred who answered the Lamplighter Company. We did not expect to need a second hundred. We were wrong within the season — the dark tests every wick it can reach, and a kingdom held together by will alone cannot afford a single window going dark unnoticed.

So the doctrine was born, plain as the charter that founded it: light on the hour, snuff on the hour, and a company for every street so that no candle in Amarath ever burns, or fails to burn, alone. Three centuries on, I am told the doctrine has not changed one line. I believe it. Doctrine is the only thing in this kingdom that does not have to remember to keep burning.'

title: Fragment: The Guttering of Threadneedle Row
body:
A LAMPLIGHTER'S LOG, RECOVERED FROM A WATCH-POST ON THREADNEEDLE ROW

'Third bell, and Threadneedle Row has gone dark house by house — not snuffed, not stolen, just gone, the way a name goes when nobody says it long enough. I lit forty windows myself before dawn and thirty-one of them had guttered again by the time I reached the end of the street. I do not have a doctrine for a street that will not stay lit.

The company sergeant told me not to write this down. I am writing it down anyway. If a whole row can go dark and come back dark no matter how many times we light it, then the rite is not holding everything the Court says it is holding, and somebody above my rank ought to know that before the next row does the same.

I relit Threadneedle Row a fourth time before the log closed. It held until morning. I do not know if that is a victory or a postponement. In this company, I have learned, they are often the same thing.'

title: Fragment: The First Tide-Charter
body:
FOUNDING CHARTER OF THE CAUSEWAY GARRISONS — YEAR ONE OF THE RETURN

'When the border came back, it did not come back where the old surveys said it would be. It came back twenty miles further in, and it brought a tide with it that had never once touched this shore before. The Court's first order was simple: hold the line the surveys remembered, not the line the water drew.

We have held that line for three centuries now, and the water has never once agreed with us about where it runs. Every garrison here knows the old chart by heart and stands exactly where it says to stand, ankle-deep or waist-deep, whatever the tide decides that morning.

I am told this looks like stubbornness to anyone who wasn't erased along with the border. I would call it something else. A kingdom that spent three centuries being nowhere does not give up an inch of where it is now, not even to the sea that carried it back.'

title: Fragment: The Night the Waterline Moved
body:
A CAUSEWAY GUARD'S LOG, RECOVERED FROM A FLOODED WATCH-POST

'Third watch, and the waterline has moved again — not risen, moved, the whole border sliding forty yards inland between one bell and the next like the tide forgot where it was supposed to stop. I marked the new line myself before dawn, same as the charter says, and by midmorning the old line was showing through the shallows again, plain as if it had never left.

The garrison captain told me not to write this down. I am writing it down anyway. If the border cannot decide where it is from one bell to the next, then the Court's charts are not holding what they claim to hold, and somebody above my rank ought to know that before the Worldmender's people find it out for themselves.

I marked the waterline a third time before the log closed. It held until the tide turned. I do not know if a border that moves is still a border, or just a grief that hasn't finished deciding where to stand.'

title: Fragment: The First Stillness Charter
body:
FOUNDING CHARTER OF THE REED GARRISONS — YEAR ONE OF THE RETURN

'When the marsh came back, it came back holding a stillness no living surveyor had ever measured — water so calm it kept the sky's exact shape from three centuries gone, never once rippling to match the sky that hangs there now. The Court's first order was simple: guard the reflection, not the water.

We have guarded that reflection for three centuries, and it has never once needed our protection. What it needs, we came to understand rather slower than the charter implies we should have, is our company. A memory kept perfectly still for three hundred years gets lonely in ways no rite anticipated.

I am told this looks like superstition to anyone who wasn't erased along with the marsh. I would call it something else. A kingdom that spent three centuries being nowhere does not begrudge its own memory a garrison to keep it company, even one it never asked for.'

title: Fragment: The Night the Sky Stopped Matching
body:
A REED-GUARD'S LOG, RECOVERED FROM A STILLWATER WATCH-POST

'Third watch, and the marsh has stopped reflecting the sky overhead — not gone dark, stopped matching, the water still showing stars in patterns the sky above hasn't worn since before the void. I checked the surface myself before dawn, same as the charter says, and by midmorning the water had gone back to holding the true sky again, plain as if it had never wandered.

The garrison captain told me not to write this down. I am writing it down anyway. If the marsh can choose which sky to remember from one bell to the next, then the Court's charts are not holding what they claim to hold, and somebody above my rank ought to know that before the Worldmender's people find it out for themselves.

I checked the reflection a third time before the log closed. It matched the true sky until dawn. I do not know if a memory that wanders is still a memory, or just a grief that hasn't finished deciding which world to keep.'

title: Fragment: The First Ceremony of Masks
body:
FOUNDING CHARTER OF THE HOLLOW COURT'S CEREMONY — YEAR ONE OF THE RETURN

'When the Court came back, it came back to a hall of mirrors that showed nothing — not one noble's face reflected true, because not one noble remembered their face well enough for the glass to have anything to copy. The first Chamberlain did not call this a crisis. He called it an opportunity, and the charter says so in his own hand.

We were given masks not to hide what was lost, but to have something to be seen wearing while we grieved it properly. A silver face is not a lie if everyone in the hall knows it is silver. It is only a lie if you let someone believe there was ever a different one underneath worth missing more than the ceremony that replaced it.

I am told this looks like cowardice to anyone who wasn't erased along with the Court. I would call it something else. A kingdom that spent three centuries being nowhere does not owe the world its face back before it is ready to wear one.'

title: Fragment: The Last Unmasked Face
body:
A COURTIER'S LOG, RECOVERED FROM A SEALED ANTECHAMBER

'Third ceremony of the season, and Lady Ashgrave took off her mask in front of the whole hall — not dropped it, not lost it, took it off on purpose, and stood there with a face none of us could place against any noble we remembered serving. The Chamberlain did not stop her. He only watched, the way the whole ceremony has learned to watch anything that breaks its own rule.

I have never seen a room hold so still. Nobody clapped. Nobody looked away either. She stood unmasked until the candles guttered, and then she put the mask back on herself, and nobody in that hall has spoken of it since, though I notice half of them have stopped meeting each other's eyes at the door the way they used to.

I am not certain what she proved. I am only certain that for one ceremony, this Court remembered it used to have faces worth keeping, and I do not think it has forgiven her for reminding it.'

title: Fragment: The First Storage Order
body:
FOUNDING CHARTER OF THE FROST GARRISONS — YEAR ONE OF THE RETURN

'When the Court understood what the void had cost Amarath, it did not simply grieve the loss. It took inventory. Among the things catalogued and found intact was a season — an entire winter, whole and unspent, that the kingdom never got to have before the Fracture erased it.

The Chamberlain's charter was blunt about what came next: store it. Do not spend a season the kingdom is owed on an ordinary year. Keep it cold, keep it waiting, and release it only when Amarath needs a winter more than it needs an ordinary one.

Three centuries on, I am told the storage has never once been breached early. I believe it. A kingdom that spent three centuries being nowhere does not waste the one season it has left over, no matter how badly the ordinary winters have wanted it back.'

title: Fragment: The Night the Storage Cracked
body:
A FROST-GUARD'S LOG, RECOVERED FROM AN ICEHOUSE WATCH-POST

'Third watch, and the storage seal has cracked for the first time in three centuries — not shattered, cracked, a hairline fracture no wider than a blade of frost, and already the corridor beyond it is ten degrees colder than the charter says it should be. I sealed it myself before dawn, same as the order says, and by midmorning the crack had spread another inch regardless.

The garrison captain told me not to write this down. I am writing it down anyway. If the storage cannot hold a season that was never meant to be spent yet, then the Court's charts are not holding what they claim to hold, and somebody above my rank ought to know that before the Worldmender's people find it out for themselves.

I sealed the crack a third time before the log closed. It held until the tide turned colder. I do not know if a season that wants out is still being kept, or just a grief that has finally run out of patience.'
